title: The Roman Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Roman Empire from Augustus to the last emperor in the West: Teutoburg Forest, Britannia and Boudica, Pompeii, Trajan’s conquests, Hadrian’s Wall, Alexandria, Marcus Aurelius on the Danube, the third-century crisis, Diocletian, Constantine and the sack of Rome to the fall of the West in 476.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Roman Empire, 27 BCE to 476 CE
note: Based mainly on Tacitus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Pliny the Younger, the Historia Augusta (used with care), Ammianus Marcellinus and Augustine, on inscriptions and coins, and on archaeology; each chapter says which it follows. Ancient figures for armies and deaths are often too large and are given as theirs. Native names are Latin. The map is stylised and not to scale; coasts are drawn as they are today. The eastern half of the empire carries on in the Byzantine Empire story. Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: Augustus and the Roman peace
steps.text: In 27 BCE Octavian became Augustus, “the revered one”. He called himself first citizen (princeps) and kept the Senate, but commanded the army, the provinces and the treasury. He ended a century of civil war, and the long peace that followed is called the Pax Romana. He died in 14 CE, and his stepson Tiberius succeeded him.
steps.today: Today: Rome, Italy; Augustus’s mausoleum stands near the Tiber.

steps.title: Teutoburg Forest
steps.text: In 9 CE three legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus were ambushed and destroyed in Germania by a coalition led by Arminius, a Roman-trained chieftain of the Cherusci. Roman writers say Augustus cried out for his lost legions. Rome never again tried to hold the lands beyond the Rhine. Kalkriese is the leading candidate site, but it is not certain.
steps.today: Today: near Osnabrück, Lower Saxony, Germany; Kalkriese has a museum.

steps.title: Britannia, Londinium and Boudica
steps.text: Claudius invaded Britain in 43 CE, with some 40,000 troops. Londinium grew into a port on the Thames. In 60 or 61 CE Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a revolt that burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium. Tacitus, who tells it, says about 70,000 died, a figure that is disputed. The governor Suetonius Paulinus crushed the rising.
steps.today: Today: London, England; a layer of burnt red earth marks the revolt.

steps.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
steps.text: Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pumice. Pliny the Younger described it in letters to Tacitus; his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died on the shore. The dig shows houses, shops and graffiti as they were. The traditional date is 24 August, though some finds favour the autumn.
steps.today: Today: near Naples, Italy; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Trajan conquers Dacia
steps.text: Trajan, born in Hispania, was the first emperor from the provinces. After two hard wars, in 101 to 102 and 105 to 106 CE, he conquered Dacia and its gold mines, which paid for Trajan’s Column in Rome. Veterans and settlers poured in, and Romanian, a language descended from Latin, is spoken there still.
steps.today: Today: Romania; the Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains are a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The empire at its widest
steps.text: In 116 CE Trajan led his army from Antioch down the Euphrates, took the Parthian capital Ctesiphon and sailed to the Persian Gulf. Revolts broke out behind him, and he died in 117 CE. His successor Hadrian gave up the new eastern provinces. The empire was never wider than at Trajan’s death.
steps.today: Today: south of Baghdad, Iraq; the vault of Taq Kasra, a later palace, still stands.

steps.title: Hadrian marks the frontier
steps.text: Hadrian chose to hold the empire’s limits, not widen them. After touring the provinces he ordered a wall across northern Britain in 122 CE, about 80 Roman miles (117 km) from the Tyne to the Solway, with forts and milecastles built by legionaries. Elsewhere frontiers were marked by wooden palisades, rivers and roads.
steps.today: Today: northern England; Hadrian’s Wall is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Alexandria and the grain fleet
steps.text: Egypt was Augustus’s own province, and its grain fed Rome by sea. Alexandria, with its lighthouse, the Pharos, and its great Library, was among the empire’s largest cities. Ptolemy wrote on astronomy there in the 2nd century CE. Ships also carried Indian pepper and cloth from Red Sea ports, whose trade Roman writers tell us was huge.
steps.today: Today: Alexandria, Egypt; the Pharos fell to earthquakes by the 14th century.

steps.title: Marcus Aurelius on the Danube
steps.text: Marcus Aurelius, a Stoic philosopher, spent much of his reign defending the Danube. His private notebook, now called the Meditations, was written in Greek, partly on campaign; one book is marked as written among the Quadi. The Antonine Plague, from 165 CE, killed millions, an uncertain total. His death in 180 ended the age of the “good emperors”.
steps.today: Today: near Vienna, Austria; Carnuntum is an open-air archaeological park.

steps.title: The crisis of the third century
steps.text: Between 235 and 284 CE, some twenty-five emperors, counts vary, ruled, most killed by soldiers, while invasions, plague and inflation hit. In 260 the Persian king Shapur I captured the emperor Valerian. Gaul and the desert city of Palmyra, under Queen Zenobia, broke away. Aurelian won both back by 274, then built a great wall around Rome.
steps.today: Today: Tadmur, Syria; the ruins of Palmyra were damaged in the 2010s.

steps.title: Diocletian shares the empire
steps.text: Diocletian, emperor from 284, found one ruler too few. From 293 two senior and two junior emperors, the tetrarchy, shared power, ruling from Nicomedia, Milan, Trier and Sirmium. He reorganised the provinces and in 301 tried to fix prices by edict, which failed. In 305 he retired to his palace at Split, on the Adriatic.
steps.today: Today: İzmit, Turkey, and Split, Croatia; Diocletian’s Palace is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Constantine and the Christian empire
steps.text: In 312 Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge beside Rome, crediting the Christian God. With Licinius he granted toleration in 313, the Edict of Milan. He called the Council of Nicaea in 325 and in 330 dedicated a new capital, Constantinople, on the Bosporus. Christianity became the state religion under Theodosius I in 380.
steps.today: Today: Rome, with the Arch of Constantine beside the Colosseum.

steps.title: The sack of Rome
steps.text: Visigoths under Alaric entered Rome by night on 24 August 410 and plundered it for three days. Emperors had long ruled from elsewhere, but the shock was great. Augustine began The City of God in answer to pagans who blamed Christianity. The Goths had first entered the empire as refugees fleeing the Huns.
steps.today: Today: Rome; the Aurelian Wall, which Alaric’s army passed, still stands in places.

steps.title: The last emperor in the West
steps.text: In 476 the general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna, sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. Later writers date the fall of the Western Empire here, though many people at the time saw little change. The emperors at Constantinople carried on the Roman Empire for nearly a thousand years.
steps.today: Today: Ravenna, Italy; its early Christian mosaics are a World Heritage Site.

items.role: The Roman state under emperors: from Augustus’s first citizen, the Senate kept and the army his, to Diocletian’s four rulers and Constantine’s Christian empire, until the West fell in 476.

items.name: Augustus
items.text: Born Gaius Octavius, Caesar’s great-nephew and adopted heir, he won the civil wars and ruled for more than forty years. He kept the Senate and old titles, yet held command of the army. His own account of his deeds, the Res Gestae, was inscribed in bronze and survives in copies at Ankara.

items.name: Trajan
items.text: Trajan, born in Hispania, was chosen by Nerva as heir in 97. He conquered Dacia, built a new harbour at Ostia and a great forum in Rome, and fed poor children with a public scheme. His eastern campaign carried the empire to its widest limits, and he died in Cilicia on the way home.

items.name: Hadrian
items.text: Hadrian, Trajan’s kinsman and successor, spent much of his reign travelling the provinces. He admired Greek culture, grew a beard and rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome. His wall in Britain marked a frontier. He crushed the Jewish revolt led by Bar Kokhba in 132 to 135 CE and died at Baiae.

items.name: Marcus Aurelius
items.text: Marcus Aurelius ruled with Lucius Verus at first, and then alone. He fought on the Danube and met the Antonine Plague. His Meditations, notes to himself on duty and mortality, are a classic of Stoic thought. His son Commodus, who followed him, is often seen as the start of the empire’s troubles.

items.name: Diocletian
items.text: Diocletian, a soldier of humble birth from Dalmatia, took power in 284. He split the empire’s rule among four men, doubled the provinces, and reformed taxes and the coinage. He also launched the last and worst persecution of Christians, from 303. He is among the few emperors to retire, living on in Split.

items.name: Constantine
items.text: Proclaimed emperor at York in 306, Constantine reunited the empire by 324. After Milvian Bridge he supported the Christian church, funded great basilicas and presided at Nicaea. He founded Constantinople and was baptised only on his deathbed. Historians still debate how deep his faith was. The Orthodox churches call him a saint.
